title: Iron, Nitrogen and an Electron Ferry: Why Transition Metals Are Good Catalysts
subject: Chemistry
objective: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up by lowering its activation energy. Transition metals are good catalysts because they can adopt multiple oxidation states and form complexes. On a metal surface (iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, nickel in hydrogenation) reactant molecules bond to surface atoms using 3d and 4s electrons, so their concentration rises and their bonds weaken. In solution, Fe³⁺ ferries electrons between I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻ (2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂; 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻) and is regenerated.

tf.q: A catalyst is used up during the reaction.
tf.explain: It is regenerated; the same amount is present at the end.

tf.q: A catalyst changes the enthalpy change (ΔH) of a reaction.
tf.explain: It only lowers the activation energy.

tf.q: Nickel is used as a catalyst for the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
tf.explain: Oils become solid fats such as vanaspati ghee.

ar.r: They can adopt multiple oxidation states and form complexes / bonds with reactants.

ar.a: Fe³⁺ catalyses the reaction between I⁻ and S₂O₈²⁻.
ar.r: Fe³⁺ can take an electron from I⁻ and Fe²⁺ can give it to S₂O₈²⁻.
ar.explain: It is regenerated at the end.

short.q: Give two effects of the bonding between reactant molecules and the atoms of a catalyst surface.
short.solution: The concentration of reactants at the surface increases, and the bonds in the reacting molecules weaken, so the activation energy is lowered (NCERT 4.3.12).

short.q: Explain with equations how iron(III) catalyses the reaction between iodide and persulphate ions.
short.solution: 2Fe³⁺ + 2I⁻ → 2Fe²⁺ + I₂; then 2Fe²⁺ + S₂O₈²⁻ → 2Fe³⁺ + 2SO₄²⁻. Fe³⁺ is regenerated, so it acts as a catalyst; it lets the two negative ions react via a positive ion.

short.q: Why is Zn²⁺ not a good catalyst for the iodide–persulphate reaction?
short.solution: Zinc shows only the +2 oxidation state (3d¹⁰), so Zn²⁺ cannot take an electron and give it back; it cannot shuttle electrons between the reactants.
